ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

elbow imaging — clinical pattern 5

A patient lands directly on the posterior elbow and cannot extend comfortably. The lateral radiograph shows a clear fracture through the posterior proximal ulna, separating the triceps-bearing process. The radial head remains aligned with the capitellum. Which bony injury is shown?

  1. Olecranon fracture
  2. Traumatic elbow effusion with possible occult fracture
  3. Radial head dislocation
  4. Extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture
  5. Normal radiographic elbow alignment
Answer and explanation

Olecranon fracture

A fracture through the posterior proximal ulna at the triceps insertion identifies an olecranon injury.

Option explanations

Olecranon fracture: A fracture through the posterior proximal ulna at the triceps insertion identifies an olecranon injury.

Traumatic elbow effusion with possible occult fracture: A visible posterior fat pad after trauma suggests an effusion and should prompt consideration of an occult intra-articular fracture. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Radial head dislocation: A radiocapitellar line that fails to intersect the capitellum on adequate views raises concern for radial head malalignment. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture: Posterior displacement of the distal humeral fragment can place the capitellum behind the anterior humeral line. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Normal radiographic elbow alignment: Normal radiocapitellar alignment and appropriate anterior humeral-line intersection support normal alignment but do not exclude every injury. This is not the pattern specified in this case.
